extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians, mathematics students, and readers interested in the philosophy/values of mathematical research
extracted.subtask_description: General criteria for assessing the value of mathematical research and a mathematician's life, emphasizing utility, aesthetic merit, originality, teaching, and moral distance from practical harms. Drawn from Hardy's reflections on what makes mathematical work worth creating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility / practical applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: It is undeniable that a good deal of elementary mathematics ... has considerable practical utility. ... The 'real' mathematics of the 'real' mathematicians ... is almost wholly 'useless'. It is not possible to justify the life of any genuine professional mathematician on the ground of the 'utility' of his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat practical utility as a distinct dimension: elementary mathematics often has clear applications, but the highest mathematical work is often 'useless' in the practical sense. Hardy argues that lack of utility does not invalidate the worth of pure mathematics and that one should not attempt to justify a mathematical life solely by utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic value / beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: These parts of mathematics are, on the whole, rather dull; they are just the parts which have the least aesthetic value. The 'real' mathematics ... is almost wholly 'useless' (and this is as true of 'applied' as of 'pure' mathematics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic merit (elegance, beauty, depth) is presented as the central value of 'real' mathematics and is often inversely correlated with immediate practical usefulness. Evaluate mathematical work for its intrinsic mathematical beauty and conceptual elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original contribution / creation worth creating
rubrics_metrics.description: I have added something to knowledge, and helped others to add more; and that these somethings have a value which differs in degree only, and not in kind, from that of the creations of the great mathematicians ... I have just one chance of escaping a verdict of complete triviality, that I may be judged to have created something worth creating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary defence of a mathematical life is the production of original, lasting contributions. Assess whether the work genuinely adds to knowledge and whether that addition is of a kind comparable (in degree) to lasting creative achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and influence on others
rubrics_metrics.description: I have helped to train other mathematicians, but mathematicians of the same kind as myself, and their work has been, so far at any rate as I have helped them to it, as useless as my own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider pedagogical and mentorship contributions: training new mathematicians is a form of impact. Hardy notes this counts toward a mathematician's life-value, even if trainees pursue similarly 'useless' directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/ethical remoteness (protection from misuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science works for evil as well as for good (and particularly, of course, in time of war); and both Gauss and less mathematicians may be justified in rejoicing that there is one science at any rate, and that their own, whose very remoteness from ordinary human activities should keep it gentle and clean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a field's remoteness from ordinary practical activities reduces the likelihood of harmful applications; Hardy treats this remoteness as a moral advantage and a reason pure mathematicians might value 'uselessness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal comfort/happiness versus broader value
rubrics_metrics.description: My choice was right, then, if what I wanted was a reasonable comfortable and happy life. But solicitors and stockbrokers and bookmakers often lead comfortable and happy lives, and it is very difficult to see how the world is richer for their existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal satisfaction or economic comfort is acknowledged but treated as insufficient justification for claiming broader societal value. Distinguish between private contentment and contributions of lasting public or cultural worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy with the arts / artistic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The case for my life, then, or for that of any one else who has been a mathematician in the same sense which I have been one, is this: that I have added something to knowledge ... and that these somethings have a value which differs in degree only, and not in kind, from that of the creations of the great mathematicians, or of any of the other artists ... who have left some kind of memorial behind them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge mathematical achievements similarly to works of art: focus on creative, memorial, and cultural value rather than only instrumental outcomes. Place mathematical creativity on a continuum with other artistic creations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding the anti-pattern of boasting about 'uselessness'
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sometimes suggested that pure mathematicians glory in the uselessness of their work ... I am sure that Gauss’s saying (if indeed it be his) has been rather crudely misinterpreted. If the theory of numbers could be employed for any practical and obviously honourable purpose ... then surely neither Gauss nor any other mathematician would have been so foolish as to decry or regret such applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not misread claims about 'uselessness' as prideful rejection of usefulness. Hardy warns against crude interpretation: mathematicians do not despise useful, honourable applications; the point is that 'useless' work may be valued for other reasons (aesthetic, moral).
